activity.role: Entu High Priestess of Sin at Ur
activity.notes: Ennigaldi-Nanna was a daughter of Nabonidus, the last king of the Neo-Babylonian Empire. Nabonidus' own inscriptions record that after divination he elevated his daughter to the revived office of entu high priestess of the moon god Sin/Nanna at Ur and gave her the ceremonial name En-nigaldi-Nanna. The appointment belongs to Nabonidus' second regnal year, 554 BCE. ATLAS models her as serving the Neo-Babylonian Empire through a royal-religious office rather than as a sovereign ruler. The terminal year 539 BCE is the end of the Neo-Babylonian political context after the Persian conquest and is not asserted as her death date or necessarily the end of her priestly life. A sixth-century BCE antiquities collection excavated in the complex associated with her has often been interpreted since Leonard Woolley as the world's earliest known museum and Ennigaldi-Nanna is therefore frequently called an early or the first museum curator; this is a historically important modern archaeological interpretation, not a contemporaneous title or a securely documented personal act, so ATLAS does not use 'curator' as her primary Activity role. The user-supplied label Babylon is normalized to Neo-Babylonian Empire.

sources.title: Nabonidus 34 — Royal Inscriptions of Babylonia Online (RIBo/ORACC)
sources.citation_text: The royal inscription records the divine request for an entu-priestess and Nabonidus' response concerning the appointment of his daughter at Ur.

sources.title: RINBE 2, Nabonidus 34 composite — Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative
sources.citation_text: The CDLI edition translates Nabonidus' statement that he raised his own daughter to the high-priestess office and named her En-Nigaldi-Nanna; the inscription's astronomical and regnal context supports the 554 BCE appointment.

sources.title: The Giparu at Ur — Iraq 37 (1975)
sources.citation_text: Penelope Weadock identifies the giparu as the official residence of the entu-priestess and states that Nabonidus revived the long-lapsed office and established his daughter Ennigaldi-Nanna as entu at Ur.

sources.title: Architecture on Display — Les Cahiers de la recherche architecturale urbaine et paysagere
sources.citation_text: The article discusses the sixth-century BCE antiquities display associated with Ennigaldi-Nanna and the modern interpretation of it as the earliest known exhibition or museum, while making clear that little of the display itself can be reconstructed.
